definition: A decoding strategy (also called nucleus sampling) that samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p.
details: Unlike top-k, top-p dynamically adjusts how many tokens are considered based on the shape of the probability distribution, often producing more natural and varied text.

explainer.lead: Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, draws from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p. It matters because it adapts the candidate set to the distribution instead of fixing its size.

tiers.eli5: You keep adding the model's favourite next words until they cover most of the likelihood, then choose from that shortlist. The list grows or shrinks as needed.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers often prefer it to top-k for natural, varied text because the cutoff tracks distribution shape. A pitfall is setting p too high on factual tasks, letting unlikely tokens creep in.
tiers.paperLevel: Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds threshold p. Limits: the cutoff depends on the probability shape, so behavior varies by context.

explainer.example: With p=0.9, the model samples only from the tokens that together account for 90 percent of the probability mass.

citation.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
